title: useVirtualList
body:
## Bullet 3 ⭐ Virtual list — 500+ DOM nodes → 20/30 FPS → 60 FPS > Built the infinite scroll Feed for the Xiaodu App homepage (daily PV 5M+) based on Haokan Video (React 16.8 + Webpack 4). Implemented virtual list rendering via a custom useVirtualList Hook with IntersectionObserver, reducing DOM nodes from 500+ to ~20 and improving scroll frame rate from 30 FPS to a stable 60 FPS. - The browser's rendering pipeline: JS → Style → Layout → Paint (record draw commands) → Layerize → Raster → Composite, with a 16.67ms budget per frame at 60 FPS. **Paint does not draw pixels, and layerization comes *after* paint** - How a virtual list works: the data layer (`list`) only grows, while the render layer (`visibleItems`) keeps only the nodes near the viewport. React's `key` diff mounts and unmounts the DOM for you — there is no hand-written teardown. - The sentinel pattern: an empty `div` at the bottom, watched by `IntersectionObserver`, triggers the next page. It works alongside the virtual list; the two are separate mechanisms — data layer and render layer. - Why `translateY` and not `top`: `transform` **always skips layout** — that is its entire advantage over `top`. "Composite only" requires the element to actually have its own compositing layer, so **do not just answer "GPU accelerated"**. - Why the index works as a key here: the real rule is "a key must uniquely and stably identify one row". In a virtual list, `list` is append-only, so the index is naturally stable and using it is correct. - `getBoundingClientRect` forces synchronous layout: any API that reads geometry makes the browser flush the pending layout work immediately. Alternating writes and reads is the classic trap. #### ① Why 500 DOM nodes drop frames The browser's rendering pipeline (**learn this**): ``` JS → Style → Layout → Paint (record draw commands) → Layerize → Raster → Composite → Display ``` Every frame has to get through the whole pipeline, in 16.67ms if you want 60 FPS. - **JS**: run code, trigger React reconciliation, update state - **Style**: work out each element's final CSS (inheritance, cascade, selector matching) - **Layout (reflow)**: compute each element's **geometry** — position and size. 500 DOM nodes means 500 geometry calculations, and one layout pass can take 5–10ms. - **Paint**: ⚠️ **it does not draw pixels.** It produces a **display list** of draw commands — "rounded rect here, line of text there". Cost scales with the number and complexity of draw items. - **Layerize**: decides how many compositing layers to cut. ⚠️ **Layers are not produced by paint — this is a separate step, and it comes after paint.** The [RenderingNG architecture doc](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/chromium/renderingng-architecture) lists the stages as `… Layout → Pre-paint → Paint → Commit → Layerize → Raster …` - **Raster**: actually executes the draw commands into **bitmap tiles**. **Text rasterisation, shadows and rounded corners are slow here, not in paint.** - **Composite**: the compositor thread packs the rastered tiles into a frame and hands it to the GPU process. **The one line to remember**: paint records draw commands, raster turns them into tiles, composite assembles tiles into a frame. **"Paint draws pixels" and "paint produces layers" are both wrong.** > The widely circulated old diagram (`Recalc Styles → Layout → Update Layer Tree → Paint → Composite`, with layerization *before* paint) shows the architecture **before the CompositeAfterPaint rewrite**. That `Update Layer Tree` stage no longer exists; the document is painted into a display list first, and PaintArtifactCompositor layerizes from it. When challenged with that diagram, naming CompositeAfterPaint is worth more than arguing about the order. What hurts with 500 nodes: - First render: style + layout + paint all multiplied by 500 — the first screen can take hundreds of milliseconds - Scrolling: each scroll may trigger layout (`sticky`, `getBoundingClientRect`), and the more nodes there are, the more visible the jank - Memory: each node costs kilobytes, so a few hundred nodes is a few megabytes #### ② The core idea The user can only see 10–20 items at once, so keep only those in the DOM and let the rest merely pretend to exist. ``` data (1000 rows) ↓ viewport (0–800px) ← what the user sees ↓ DOM holds the 10 visible items plus 2 overscan above and below ≈ 14 ``` While scrolling: 1. Work out the scroll position 2. Compute which rows should be showing — say 300 to 314 3. Remove the DOM for the previous 280–294 and insert 300–314 4. Position the new items with `translateY` The key point: **the `list` array in the data layer only ever grows** (pagination appends), but **the number of DOM nodes does not grow with it**. They are two entirely decoupled pieces of state. Mounting and unmounting is not hand-written `removeChild`; every scroll recomputes which indices should show right now, and React's `key` diff detaches whatever is not in that set. A `key` outside the new visible range simply is not created on the next render, so the old node unmounts. #### ③ The spacer that keeps the scrollbar honest With only 14 items in the DOM, how does the browser know the scrollbar should be 1,000 rows long? Set the outer container's height to `1000 × itemHeight` — the total of all items — and position each item with `position: absolute` and `translateY`: ```js
{/* holds the scrollbar open */}
row 300
row 301
...
``` #### ④ Why `transform: translateY` and not `top` | Property | What it triggers | |---|---| | `top` / `left` / `width` / `height` / `margin` / `padding` | Layout (reflow, the most expensive) + paint + composite | | `color` / `background` / `border-radius` | Paint (repaint) + composite | | `transform` / `opacity` | **Does not trigger layout.** "Composite only" requires its own compositing layer | ⚠️ **One fact about this implementation first, or the rest reads backwards.** In the hook, `offsetTop = i * itemHeight` is row *i*'s absolute position within the whole list — it has nothing to do with `scrollTop`. **Once a card is mounted its transform value never changes until it is recycled**; what changes while scrolling is the container's native `scrollTop`. So there is **no "transform changing every frame"** here. **So where does `transform` beat `top`? At the moment a new card mounts.** As the window slides down and the next few cards need positioning, `top` costs one layout pass; `transform` does not enter layout at all. **That is one reflow saved per window shift, not per frame.** **⭐ Do not answer "GPU accelerated".** The follow-up is "did you promote it to a layer?", and if you cannot answer, you are caught. The accurate version is three sentences: - **Layout is always skipped** — that is the whole of `transform`'s advantage over `top`, promoted or not. - **If promoted** (`will-change: transform`, a 3D transform, an animation the compositor took over), changing the transform matrix happens entirely on the compositor thread and reuses the already-rastered tiles, so the animation stays smooth even when a long task blocks the main thread. - **If not promoted**, the element shares a layer with others, and moving it means **that layer's tiles must be re-rastered** — the main thread is involved again. **Promotion buys nothing here, and actively hurts**: the transform value never changes, so there is no repeated matrix update to optimise; putting `will-change: transform` on dozens of cards buys dozens of layers and a pile of GPU memory. Promotion is worth it only when one element's transform changes repeatedly — animation, dragging, custom inertial scrolling. **The GPU acceleration of scrolling itself is free**: native container scrolling is the compositor thread translating already-rastered tiles. It requires nothing from you and has nothing to do with whether you use `transform`. #### ⑤ IntersectionObserver and the sentinel: when the *data* layer should load more The old way: listen to `scroll` and call `getBoundingClientRect()` to see whether an element is in the viewport. Every scroll could run that check dozens of times, which loads the main thread, and `getBoundingClientRect` forces layout. `IntersectionObserver` is a native API that calls you back asynchronously when **an element enters or leaves the viewport**. It does not block the main thread and does not trigger layout. ```js const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => { entries.forEach(entry => { if (entry.isIntersecting) { loadMore(); // fetch the next page } }); }, { root: null, rootMargin: '100px', // fire 100px early threshold: 0, }); observer.observe(document.querySelector('#loader')); // the sentinel, usually an empty div at the bottom ``` The sentinel is an empty node that displays nothing and exists only to be detected. As the user scrolls it enters the viewport → `loadMore()` fires → the next page is fetched → the rows are appended to `list` → the sentinel is still rendered at the end of the new list, and round it goes. **Keep "sentinel + IntersectionObserver" and "virtual list" clearly apart.** The first decides when the data grows (should `list` append?). The second decides which slice of it is in the DOM at any moment (`visibleItems` is a sliding window over `list`). Load a single page of 20 rows and the virtual list still renders only what is near the viewport; load 1,000 and the DOM node count still does not move. #### ⑥ A skeleton useVirtualList ```js function useVirtualList(items, itemHeight, containerHeight, overscan = 3) { const [scrollTop, setScrollTop] = useState(0); const startIndex = Math.max(0, Math.floor(scrollTop / itemHeight) - overscan); const visibleCount = Math.ceil(containerHeight / itemHeight); const endIndex = Math.min(items.length - 1, startIndex + visibleCount + overscan * 2); const visibleItems = []; for (let i = startIndex; i <= endIndex; i++) { visibleItems.push({ index: i, item: items[i], offsetTop: i * itemHeight, }); } const totalHeight = items.length * itemHeight; const containerRef = useRef(null); useEffect(() => { const el = containerRef.current; if (!el) return; const onScroll = () => setScrollTop(el.scrollTop); el.addEventListener('scroll', onScroll, { passive: true }); return () => el.removeEventListener('scroll', onScroll); }, []); return { containerRef, totalHeight, visibleItems }; } ``` Using it: ```js const { containerRef, totalHeight, visibleItems } = useVirtualList(list, 80, 600); return (
{visibleItems.map(({ index, item, offsetTop }) => (
{renderItem(item)}
))}
); ``` `passive: true` on the scroll listener matters: it tells the browser you will not call `event.preventDefault()` in the handler, so it can start scrolling immediately instead of waiting for the JavaScript to finish and find out. Without it, scrolling feels slower to respond. #### ⑦ Why the index is fine as a key here The usual advice is "don't use the index as a key", but the point behind that rule is "a key must uniquely and stably identify one row" — there is nothing inherently wrong with an index. What the rule guards against is a list that reorders, or has items inserted or removed in the middle, while the item contents stay the same. There, the index and the actual row drift apart, React reuses the wrong component instance, and you get misplaced state and jumping animations. In a virtual list, `list` only appends — nothing is inserted in the middle and nothing reorders — so row `items[15]` is index 15 forever, whatever the user scrolls or pages. And a virtual list depends on keys entering and leaving to drive mounting and unmounting: indices that scroll out disappear, indices that scroll in appear. Using the index here is correct, and arguably closer to how the thing actually works. #### ⑧ Why getBoundingClientRect needs care Normally the browser batches DOM and CSS changes and does one layout pass before the frame is drawn. But APIs that read geometry — `getBoundingClientRect()`, `offsetTop`, `scrollHeight` — have to return an accurate, current position and size. If there are pending DOM or style changes, the browser has to apply them and run layout synchronously before it can answer. That is a **forced synchronous layout**, and it is far more expensive than ordinary JavaScript. The classic trap is alternating writes and reads: ```js // bad: every iteration forces a synchronous layout for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) { items[i].style.width = someWidth + 'px'; // write: marks it dirty console.log(items[i].getBoundingClientRect()); // read: forces layout right now } // good: read in one pass, write in another const rects = items.map(item => item.getBoundingClientRect()); items.forEach((item) => { item.style.width = someWidth + 'px'; }); ``` This is also why a virtual list should use `IntersectionObserver` rather than checking visibility with `getBoundingClientRect` inside a scroll handler — under fast scrolling the latter forces layout again and again. #### ⑨ Handling variable item heights The skeleton above assumes every item is exactly 80px, but in reality feed cards differ — some have an image, some do not. - **Option 1: estimate, then correct by measuring.** Start with an average height, measure the real height once the item mounts (`ResizeObserver`, or the ref's `.offsetHeight`), store it in a `sizeMap`, and use the measured values for later offsets. - **Option 2: an offset table.** Maintain `offsets[i] = sum of the heights of the first i items`, and binary-search for `offsets[i] <= scrollTop < offsets[i+1]` when scrolling to a position. TanStack Virtual's `measureElement` is a combination of both, and a hand-rolled implementation usually lands in the same place. #### ⑩ RAIL and the 60 FPS budget, one level deeper - 60 FPS = 1000ms / 60 ≈ 16.67ms per frame - JavaScript really only gets about 10ms of that; the rest belongs to style, layout, paint, composite, and the browser's own scheduling. Go over budget and you drop a frame — and it takes several dropped frames in a row before the user calls it janky. - **RAIL**: **R**esponse (respond to input within 100ms), **A**nimation (16ms per frame), **I**dle (leave the main thread free for the browser), **L**oad (interactive within 1s). #### ⑪ 30 → 60 FPS: which steps actually did the work - **Fewer DOM nodes**: layout drops from around 10ms to around 0.5ms, and that time inside the frame goes to everything else - **`translateY` instead of `top`**: each time the window advances, positioning the newly mounted cards does not trigger layout — that saves **one reflow per window shift** (not per frame; the transform value is fixed once mounted) - **`passive: true`**: the scroll event no longer blocks the browser's compositing - **`IntersectionObserver` instead of scroll-based checks**: removes the per-scroll `getBoundingClientRect`, and with it the forced synchronous layout Those four are four different dimensions — node count, positioning, event handling, visibility detection. If someone asks which step produced the improvement, breaking it down like this holds up far better than "we used a virtual list". #### ⑫ Proving that off-screen nodes really are destroyed There is no teardown function. Destruction falls out of React's `key` diff: every scroll recomputes which indices should show, and any `key` not in `visibleItems` simply is not created on the next render. To see it with your own eyes, add a cleanup in the item component: ```js function FeedCard({ item }) { useEffect(() => { console.log(`mount: item ${item.id}`); return () => console.log(`unmount: item ${item.id}`); // prints when it scrolls out }, []); return
{/* ... */}
; } ``` While scrolling, the console prints "mount: item 15" followed by "unmount: item 2" over and over. That is the most direct code-level evidence that nodes leaving the screen are destroyed. #### ⑬ Going deeper - **Uneven item heights**: see ⑨ above. - **Keyboard navigation and focus**: when a recycled item's DOM disappears, focus goes with it. Remember the focused index and restore it on remount, or use `contain: layout` to hide offscreen content without actually removing it. - **Lazy-loading images**: a virtual list mounts only what is visible, which is lazy loading already. Combine it with native `loading="lazy"`, or wrap each image in its own `IntersectionObserver`. - **Dynamic content** (expanding comments changes the height): observe each item with `ResizeObserver`, update `sizeMap` when the height changes, and recompute the offsets. - **Does a virtual list hurt SEO?** Yes. Only the visible items are in the DOM, so a crawler never sees the rest. Either skip virtualisation for SEO-sensitive pages, or fall back to SSR — emit the full content in the HTML and virtualise once the client takes over. - **Why not `content-visibility: auto`?** It is a newer CSS feature that lets the browser skip layout and paint for invisible items — a lighter alternative that suits small and medium lists. Tens of thousands of rows still need real virtualisation. - **White flashes on fast scrolling**: increase the overscan buffer; or degrade to a static placeholder at high scroll speeds; or pre-render a skeleton. - **Infinite scroll vs pagination**: infinite scroll feels smooth but makes it hard to return to a position; pagination is clear and the URL can be shared and revisited. A middle path is updating the URL hash as you scroll, so the back button works. #### ⑭ One correction "500+ → ~20" is better stated as: **the DOM node count is held in a constant range** — the visible items plus overscan above and below, in practice around 100–150 — **and does not keep growing as the user scrolls and the data piles up**. It is not an absolute "it becomes 20". A virtual list normally carries overscan to avoid blank space during fast scrolling; rendering the viewport and nothing else tends to flicker. Before writing a number like that down, be clear about how it was measured — recording the scroll in Chrome DevTools' Performance panel, or just counting with `document.querySelectorAll('*').length`. --- ## Debounce in depth — leading, trailing, and cancel Earlier I only wrote the most basic form: run n milliseconds after the last trigger. Real situations usually need a more flexible combination — should it run immediately on the first trigger, should it run again after things stop, and can a queued call be cancelled from outside. #### ① What each of the three is for - **leading**: run immediately on the first trigger, no waiting. Click protection needs the first press to give feedback at once. - **trailing**: run once, some time after the triggers stop. A search box needs to wait until the user has finished typing. - **cancel**: abandon a queued call from outside. On unmount or a route change, so a callback does not fire after the page is gone. #### ② A correct implementation (every trap is in here) ```js function debounce(fn, wait, immediate = false) { let timer = null; function debounced(...args) { const callNow = immediate && !timer; // is this the first call of a new round? clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(() => { timer = null; // crucial: reset so the next round can decide afresh if (!immediate) fn.apply(this, args); // in immediate mode, do not run again here }, wait); if (callNow) fn.apply(this, args); // run this one right away } debounced.cancel = function () { clearTimeout(timer); timer = null; }; return debounced; } ``` #### ③ Two easy mistakes - **`timer` must be reset to `null` when it fires.** Without the reset, `immediate && !timer` is only ever true once in the function's whole life — once `timer` has been assigned, it never goes back to `null` unless you clear it. Leading behaviour would work on the very first call and never again, no matter how long you wait between triggers. This is a real bug and easy to miss. - **Leading and trailing must not both run for the same trigger.** Without the `if (!immediate)` check inside the `setTimeout` callback, a single trigger in `immediate: true` mode runs twice — once immediately, once `wait` milliseconds later. `!immediate` makes the two paths exclusive: in immediate mode, `setTimeout` only counts down and resets the timer, it does not call `fn`. #### ④ Why cancel needs both `clearTimeout` and `timer = null` `timer` is just a JavaScript variable holding the numeric ID `setTimeout` returned. Setting it to `null` only throws away your receipt; the timer the browser registered is untouched and will still fire. The call that actually cancels it is `clearTimeout(timer)`. You need both: `clearTimeout` to cancel the browser's timer, and `timer = null` to keep the internal state consistent so the next `immediate && !timer` check is correct. `clearTimeout` can only cancel a timer that has not fired yet and has not been pushed into the macrotask queue — once the callback is in the task queue it is too late. In practice, though, `cancel()` fires on unmount or a route change, which is comfortably inside the safe window, so this edge is not worth worrying about. --- ## The toolchain for diagnosing production problems #### ① Sentry, automated On every release, CI uploads that build's source maps under the release version and archives them — privately, never deployed publicly, so the source cannot be reconstructed from the map files. When the front-end SDK reports an error it carries the current release version, and Sentry matches it against the right map file and translates the minified stack into readable filenames and line numbers. No human step anywhere. The one requirement is uploading the right maps under the right release. If the release number does not match, or the upload was skipped, the translation fails and you are left staring at minified positions. #### ② git bisect — automated binary search When working out which commit introduced a bug, do not walk the commits one by one. Mark a version that is known bad and one that is known good, verify only the midpoint each time, and you find the commit in roughly `log2(n)` steps instead of `n`. ``` git bisect start git bisect bad HEAD git bisect good v1.2.0 git bisect run npm test # supply a script that decides automatically; no manual step at all ``` This assumes you have a fast way to decide whether a build is broken — a test case that reproduces it locally. Otherwise each check means a full deploy and the advantage evaporates. #### ③ Feature flags — decoupling "shipped" from "live" Being able to switch something off in seconds comes from separating "is this code deployed" from "is this feature shown to users". The code can already be in production while a remote config decides whether it takes effect. When something breaks you change the config — no redeploy, and it takes seconds. Rolling back code means a full build and deploy, which takes minutes. How to do a percentage rollout: hash the user ID into the range 0–99, and treat `bucket < percentage` as in. The hash is deterministic, so a given user's bucket never changes, which means widening the rollout — 1% to 10%, say — keeps the original users inside the new range instead of reshuffling everyone. --- ## Reviewing a full-stack project's choices — tRPC, Zod, React Hook Form Looking back at a full-stack project built on Next.js + tRPC + Zod + React Hook Form, the problems these tools solve turn out to be layered, not overlapping. #### ① tRPC solves "front-end and back-end types drift apart", and it is not a heavyweight RPC protocol The RPC in the name suggests something like gRPC — a custom binary protocol, cross-language, heavy. Underneath, tRPC is ordinary HTTP and JSON, indistinguishable in the network tab from a `fetch` you wrote yourself. The magic is entirely **compile-time**: the backend router's type is exported with `export type`, the front end brings it in with `import type` (types only, no runtime code — that import is erased at build time), and the TypeScript compiler follows that chain to infer the shape of what a given procedure returns. The IDE underlines mistakes and the build fails, without anyone hand-writing an interface to describe a response. The one prerequisite: front end and back end must live in the same repository or monorepo so they can import each other's types. That has nothing inherently to do with Next.js — a separately deployed front end and back end work fine as long as the project is organised that way. #### ② Zod solves "runtime validation", a different line of defence from tRPC TypeScript's checking only exists at compile time; once the program is running the type information is gone. Data from outside — form input, API responses, requests from third-party systems — has to be validated for real at runtime. Zod's neat trick is that one schema produces both the runtime validator (`.parse` / `.safeParse`) and the TypeScript type (`z.infer`), instead of the old arrangement where an interface and a separate validation function slowly drift apart. Even with tRPC sharing types across the boundary, the server still has to run Zod before it processes a request, because a server can never trust what a client sends: someone may be calling the endpoint directly, the front-end code may be an old version, the network may have mangled something. tRPC is about developer efficiency; Zod is about runtime safety. They are layers, not duplicates. #### ③ React Hook Form solves "large forms are laggy" by taking typing out of React's render cycle The traditional approach gives every input a `useState` and an `onChange`, so every keystroke re-renders the whole parent. With enough fields, every keystroke re-renders a large form, and it lags. RHF's core idea is uncontrolled components plus refs: each input registers its DOM node into an internal ref map with `register('field')`, the browser maintains the `value` natively, and typing triggers no React render at all. Only the places that genuinely need the current value — submit, or an explicit `useWatch` subscription — read it back out of the ref map. It is the same instinct as a virtual list: do not do work you can avoid, and only do it when it is actually needed. A virtual list controls the number of DOM nodes; RHF controls how often rendering is triggered. Pair it with Zod through `zodResolver` and the same schema validates on submit, with errors landing on `formState.errors` — no hand-written validation and no manually stuffing messages into state. --- ## In summary Put together, these are the same engineering instinct showing up in different places: **don't do work you can avoid** (a virtual list does not render invisible DOM; RHF does not render on keystrokes), **prevent what can be prevented early** (Zod rejects bad data the moment it arrives; an idempotency key deduplicates at the source), and **when something does break, find it and stop the bleeding fast** (Sentry translates stacks automatically, `git bisect` halves the search, a feature flag degrades in seconds). The tools and APIs are easy enough to look up. What actually takes thinking is why a given situation calls for a given design and what a different choice would cost — which is the point of writing these notes: not remembering how to call an API, but remembering the reasoning behind the call.
